analysis.one_liner: Moves most large class-action lawsuits out of state courts and into federal court, while restricting coupon-style settlements.
analysis.headline: Became law 24 days after introduction: the Senate passed it 72-26, the House 279-149, and the President signed it on February 18, 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This law shifts most class actions worth more than $5 million involving people from different states out of state courts and into federal courts. It also adds safeguards for class members in settlements that pay with coupons instead of cash, requires notice of proposed settlements to state and federal officials, and lets corporate defendants easily move cases into federal court. State courts had often been friendlier to consumer groups suing over faulty products, hidden fees, or deceptive practices; the law made it much harder to keep those cases there.
analysis.who_benefits: Large corporations that are defendants in class actions — banks, insurers, drug makers, product manufacturers — gain the most. They can now move big class suits to federal court without the consent of all defendants, and federal courts generally certify class actions (the step that lets a case proceed as a group suit) less often and on stricter grounds, so fewer of these cases survive and the ones that do settle for less.

how_it_helps.text: Gives federal district courts original jurisdiction over class actions exceeding $5 million where plaintiffs and defendants are citizens of different states, and lets any single defendant remove such a case from state to federal court without the consent of other defendants [S3][S7].

Caps attorney fees in coupon settlements at the value of coupons actually redeemed, and bars settlements that leave class members with a net monetary loss unless the court finds nonmonetary benefits substantially outweigh it [S2][S7].

Bars settlements that pay some class members more solely because they live closer to the court, and requires notice of proposed settlements to state attorneys general and federal regulators with a 90-day waiting period before final approval [S3][S7].
The bill's own stated purposes include assuring fair recoveries for class members and 'benefiting society by encouraging innovation and lowering consumer prices' [S7].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers with class claims over defective products, hidden fees, or deceptive practices. Cases that once proceeded in state courts — where judges were often more willing to certify consumer classes and state consumer-protection law was often stronger — get moved to federal court or dismissed, so many smaller claims that are only viable as a group never get a day in court. State attorneys general also lose the oversight role they had over local class settlements.

drawbacks.text: The core change moves consumer cases to federal court, where judges apply stricter standards for certifying a class, so many group claims by consumers become impossible to bring even when the underlying conduct is real; each individual's loss is usually too small to sue over alone [S3].

The law keeps class actions out of federal court only when two-thirds or more of the class and the main defendants are from the state where the suit was filed, and lets courts decline jurisdiction in other state-centered cases; the exceptions are narrow, so most large consumer class actions shift to federal court [S3].

A House attempt to send the bill back to committee with instructions to exempt cases arising from the use of the drug Vioxx — a harm then subject to mass litigation — failed 175-249, removing one avenue for drug-injury plaintiffs to stay in state court [S9][S11].

Banks and other depository institutions got their own notice carve-out: they can satisfy the settlement-notification requirement by serving their federal regulator rather than officials in every state where class members live [S7].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coupon-settlement and notice provisions are real, modest protections against the worst settlement abuses — lawyers taking big fees while class members get nearly worthless coupons. But those provisions are secondary. The heart of the law is the jurisdictional shift, which removes consumers' most effective tool for challenging widespread corporate misconduct: the state-court class action. The value of that tool for ordinary people was much larger than the coupon abuses it corrected.

outcome.mechanism: It sailed through both chambers in under a month — passed by the Senate 72-26 on February 10 and the House 279-149 on February 17 — and the President signed it the next day.

narrative.text: Introduced January 25, 2005, the bill was reported favorably by the Senate Judiciary Committee without amendment nine days later and placed first on the Senate calendar [S9].
The Senate passed it 72-26 on February 10, with all 55 Republicans voting yes and 18 of 44 Democrats joining them [S10].
A House attempt to commit the bill with instructions to exempt Vioxx-related cases failed 175-249, and the House passed it 279-149 the same day [S9][S11][S12].
The President signed it on February 18, 2005, making it Public Law 109-2 [S9][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporate defendants — banks, insurers, drug makers, and other mass-market businesses — are better off: their most feared civil-litigation exposure, the state-court consumer class action, was sharply narrowed. Plaintiffs' class-action firms lost a major source of large cases; consumers lost the state-court forum where those cases were easiest to win.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on January 25, 2005.

for.name: Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of the Judiciary Committee without amendment on February 3, 2005, without a written report.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on February 18, 2005.

against.name: Rep. Sherrod Brown
against.what_they_did: Moved to send the bill back to committee with instructions to exempt cases arising from use of the drug Vioxx; the motion failed 175-249.

against.name: Rep. John Conyers
against.what_they_did: Offered an amendment in the nature of a substitute that received 40 minutes of debate under the rule before being set aside.

sides.party_line_note: Republicans were nearly unanimous in both chambers (53-0 in the Senate, 229-1 in the House), while most Democrats opposed it (26 of 44 Senate Democrats and 147 of 201 House Democrats voted no).

industries.industry: Corporate class-action defendants (banks, insurers, drug makers, mass-market product companies)
industries.note: The law lets any single defendant move a large interstate class action to federal court, where judges certify classes on stricter grounds, so fewer consumer group suits survive and the ones that do settle for less. That is a direct reduction in legal exposure that ordinary people had relied on to challenge widespread corporate conduct.

Class-action plaintiffs' firms lose the ability to keep most large consumer class actions in state courts, reducing the number and size of cases they can bring. Their incentive to fight these suits runs alongside consumers' interest in a forum where group claims can succeed.

The law gives banks a special carve-out in the settlement-notice rules: they satisfy notice by serving their primary federal regulator instead of officials in every state with class members, easing compliance and keeping oversight with banking-friendly regulators rather than state attorneys general.
